problems.html: Let A=(4213)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\1&3\end{pmatrix}A=(41​23​). Verify that u=(21)\mathbf{u}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}u=(21​) and w=(1−1)\mathbf{w}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}w=(1−1​) are eigenvectors, and state the eigenvalue of each. Check your two eigenvalues against trA\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\mathbf{A}trA and det⁡A\det\mathbf{A}detA.
hints: You are not solving anything here — just multiplying. Work out Au\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}Au and compare it with u\mathbf{u}u.
If Au\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}Au comes out as a multiple of u\mathbf{u}u, that multiple is itself the eigenvalue. Read it straight off.

problems.html: Write down the characteristic equation of A=(2112)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}A=(21​12​) and solve it for the eigenvalues.
hints: The characteristic equation is det⁡(A−λI)=0\det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=0det(A−λI)=0. Write down A−λI\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I}A−λI first.
For a 2×22\times22×2 matrix the determinant is ad−bcad-bcad−bc; here that gives (2−λ)2−1=0(2-\lambda)^2-1=0(2−λ)2−1=0.
(2−λ)2=1(2-\lambda)^2=1(2−λ)2=1 means 2−λ=±12-\lambda=\pm12−λ=±1 — two cases, so two eigenvalues.

problems.html: Find, by inspection, the eigenvalues of T=(570−2)\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix}5&7\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}T=(50​7−2​). Why can you read them straight off?
hints: Look at where the zero sits. What shape is this matrix?
For a triangular matrix det⁡(A−λI)\det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})det(A−λI) is just the product of the diagonal entries of A−λI\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I}A−λI.

problems.html: For the matrix A=(2112)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}A=(21​12​) of Exercise 1.2, find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue.
hints: You already have the eigenvalues from Exercise 1.2. Take one, say λ=3\lambda=3λ=3, and solve (A−λI)v=0(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}(A−λI)v=0.
A−3I=(−111−1)\mathbf{A}-3\mathbf{I}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}A−3I=(−11​1−1​). Both rows say the same thing — that is expected, and it is why the eigenvector is only fixed up to scale.
One row gives −v1+v2=0-v_1+v_2=0−v1​+v2​=0, so v2=v1v_2=v_1v2​=v1​. Any non-zero multiple of that vector will do.
problems.format: eigenvector for λ=1; then λ=3; first entry 1

problems.html: The symmetric matrix A=(210131012)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\1&3&1\\0&1&2\end{pmatrix}A=​210​131​012​​ has eigenvalues 1,2,41,2,41,2,4. Compute trA\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\mathbf{A}trA and det⁡A\det\mathbf{A}detA and confirm they agree with the sum and product of the eigenvalues.
hints: You are not asked to find the eigenvalues — you are given them. Compute the trace and determinant directly from the matrix.
The trace is the sum of the diagonal entries. Then check it against λ1+λ2+λ3\lambda_1+\lambda_2+\lambda_3λ1​+λ2​+λ3​.
The determinant should come out as λ1λ2λ3\lambda_1\lambda_2\lambda_3λ1​λ2​λ3​.

problems.html: (a) Find the eigenvalues of the quarter-turn R=(0−110)\mathbf{R}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}R=(01​−10​). (b) Using R(θ)=(cos⁡θ−sin⁡θsin⁡θcos⁡θ)\mathbf{R}(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}R(θ)=(cosθsinθ​−sinθcosθ​), write down the eigenvalues of the 60∘60^\circ60∘ rotation.
hints: Set up det⁡(R−λI)=0\det(\mathbf{R}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=0det(R−λI)=0 as usual; do not be put off when it has no real root.
You should reach λ2+1=0\lambda^2+1=0λ2+1=0. Unit 3 tells you what its roots are.

For part (b), the characteristic equation of R(θ)\mathbf{R}(\theta)R(θ) is λ2−2λcos⁡θ+1=0\lambda^2-2\lambda\cos\theta+1=0λ2−2λcosθ+1=0; solve it with the quadratic formula and use cos⁡2θ−1=−sin⁡2θ\cos^2\theta-1=-\sin^2\thetacos2θ−1=−sin2θ.
problems.format: the eigenvalues of R in (a); +i first

problems.html: For each matrix say whether it is symmetric, Hermitian, both, or neither: (i) (1225),(ii) (2i−i3),(iii) (03−30),(iv) (12+i2+i4).\text{(i)}\ \begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&5\end{pmatrix},\quad\allowbreak \text{(ii)}\ \begin{pmatrix}2&\mathrm{i}\\-\mathrm{i}&3\end{pmatrix},\quad\allowbreak \text{(iii)}\ \begin{pmatrix}0&3\\-3&0\end{pmatrix},\quad\allowbreak \text{(iv)}\ \begin{pmatrix}1&2+\mathrm{i}\\2+\mathrm{i}&4\end{pmatrix}.(i) (12​25​),(ii) (2−i​i3​),(iii) (0−3​30​),(iv) (12+i​2+i4​).
hints: Symmetric means AT=A\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{T}}=\mathbf{A}AT=A: reflect in the leading diagonal and see if nothing moves.
Hermitian means A‾T=A\overline{\mathbf{A}}^{\mathsf{T}}=\mathbf{A}AT=A — you transpose and conjugate, not just transpose. For a real matrix the two conditions coincide.
Check the diagonal entries: a Hermitian matrix must have real numbers on its diagonal.

problems.html: Decide, with a one-line reason, whether each matrix is diagonalisable: (a) (1203),(b) (3103),(c) (2002).\text{(a)}\ \begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{pmatrix},\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ \begin{pmatrix}3&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix},\qquad\allowbreak \text{(c)}\ \begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}.(a) (10​23​),(b) (30​13​),(c) (20​02​).
hints: Two distinct eigenvalues in a 2×22\times22×2 matrix is already enough to guarantee diagonalisability. Which of these have that?
When an eigenvalue is repeated you must go further and count independent eigenvectors — compute the rank of A−λI\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I}A−λI.
A repeated eigenvalue with only one independent eigenvector is defective, and the matrix is not diagonalisable.

problems.html: Let D=(200−1)\mathbf{D}=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}D=(20​0−1​). Write down D5\mathbf{D}^{5}D5 and Dk\mathbf{D}^{k}Dk for a general positive integer kkk.
hints: Multiply D\mathbf{D}D by itself once and look at what happens to each diagonal entry.
Powers of a diagonal matrix act entry by entry: the off-diagonal zeros never interact.
problems.format: the two diagonal entries of D^5, comma-separated

problems.html: A 2×22\times22×2 matrix A\mathbf{A}A has eigenpairs λ1=3, v1=(1,1)T\lambda_1=3,\ \mathbf{v}_1=(1,1)^{\mathsf{T}}λ1​=3, v1​=(1,1)T and λ2=−2, v2=(1,−1)T\lambda_2=-2,\ \mathbf{v}_2=(1,-1)^{\mathsf{T}}λ2​=−2, v2​=(1,−1)T. Write down matrices P\mathbf{P}P and D\mathbf{D}D with A=PDP−1\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{P}^{-1}A=PDP−1, and compute P−1\mathbf{P}^{-1}P−1.
hints: The eigenvectors are the columns of P\mathbf{P}P, in the same order as the eigenvalues down D\mathbf{D}D.
So P=(111−1)\mathbf{P}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}P=(11​1−1​) and D=(300−2)\mathbf{D}=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}D=(30​0−2​); now you need P−1\mathbf{P}^{-1}P−1.
Recover A\mathbf{A}A from A=PDP−1\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{P}^{-1}A=PDP−1, then check it with the trace (=1=1=1) and determinant (=−6=-6=−6).
problems.format: P⁻¹: four entries, row by row

problems.html: A transition matrix has non-negative entries and columns that sum to one. Which of these qualify? (i) (0.60.10.40.9),(ii) (0.50.50.50.6),(iii) (0.30.70.70.3).\text{(i)}\ \begin{pmatrix}0.6&0.1\\0.4&0.9\end{pmatrix},\quad\allowbreak \text{(ii)}\ \begin{pmatrix}0.5&0.5\\0.5&0.6\end{pmatrix},\quad\allowbreak \text{(iii)}\ \begin{pmatrix}0.3&0.7\\0.7&0.3\end{pmatrix}.(i) (0.60.4​0.10.9​),(ii) (0.50.5​0.50.6​),(iii) (0.30.7​0.70.3​).
hints: Two conditions must hold together: every entry ≥0\geq 0≥0, and each column — not each row — summing to exactly 111.
Check the columns, not the rows — a matrix whose rows sum to one is a different convention.

problems.html: Find the steady-state distribution of the transition matrix P=(0.60.20.40.8)\mathbf{P}=\begin{pmatrix}0.6&0.2\\0.4&0.8\end{pmatrix}P=(0.60.4​0.20.8​) (the eigenvector for λ=1\lambda=1λ=1, scaled so its entries sum to one).
hints: The steady state is the eigenvector for λ=1\lambda=1λ=1, so solve (P−I)v=0(\mathbf{P}-\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}(P−I)v=0.
P−I=(−0.40.20.4−0.2)\mathbf{P}-\mathbf{I}=\begin{pmatrix}-0.4&0.2\\0.4&-0.2\end{pmatrix}P−I=(−0.40.4​0.2−0.2​), so the two rows give the same condition: v2=2v1v_2=2v_1v2​=2v1​.
A distribution must sum to 111, so scale (1,2)(1,2)(1,2) by dividing through by 333.
problems.format: the two components as fractions, comma-separated

problems.html: For A=(4123)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}A=(42​13​) find the eigenvalues and an eigenvector for each, and verify the trace/determinant identities.
hints: Form det⁡(A−λI)=0\det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=0det(A−λI)=0: it becomes (4−λ)(3−λ)−2=0(4-\lambda)(3-\lambda)-2=0(4−λ)(3−λ)−2=0.
Expand to λ2−7λ+10=0\lambda^2-7\lambda+10=0λ2−7λ+10=0 and factorise.
The check you want: the eigenvalues should add to the trace 777 and multiply to the determinant 101010.

problems.html: Let A=(1221)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}A=(12​21​). (a) Diagonalise A=PDP−1\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{P}^{-1}A=PDP−1. (b) Hence derive a closed form for Ak\mathbf{A}^{k}Ak, valid for every positive integer kkk. (c) Check your formula at k=1k=1k=1.
hints: Eigenvalues first: (1−λ)2−4=0(1-\lambda)^2-4=0(1−λ)2−4=0, so 1−λ=±21-\lambda=\pm21−λ=±2.
Build P\mathbf{P}P from the eigenvectors and D\mathbf{D}D from the eigenvalues, keeping the order consistent.
For part (b) use An=PDnP−1\mathbf{A}^n=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}^n\mathbf{P}^{-1}An=PDnP−1 — and Dn\mathbf{D}^nDn is easy because D\mathbf{D}D is diagonal.

problems.html: A sequence satisfies xn+1=xn+2xn−1x_{n+1}=x_n+2x_{n-1}xn+1​=xn​+2xn−1​ with x0=0, x1=1x_0=0,\ x_1=1x0​=0, x1​=1 (giving 0,1,1,3,5,11,…0,1,1,3,5,11,\dots0,1,1,3,5,11,…). (a) Write the step as (xn+1xn)=A(xnxn−1)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x_{n+1}\\x_n\end{smallmatrix}\right) =\mathbf{A}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x_{n}\\x_{n-1}\end{smallmatrix}\right)(xn+1​xn​​)=A(xn​xn−1​​) and find A\mathbf{A}A and its eigenvalues. (b) Decompose the start vector in the eigenbasis and obtain a closed form for xnx_nxn​.
hints: A recurrence that reaches two steps back becomes a one-step matrix recurrence once you carry both terms in the vector.
Read the matrix off the two identities xn+1=xn+2xn−1x_{n+1}=x_n+2x_{n-1}xn+1​=xn​+2xn−1​ and xn=xnx_n=x_nxn​=xn​: the second row simply copies the first entry down.
For (b), write the start vector as a combination of the two eigenvectors. Each one is then scaled by its own eigenvalue to the nnn-th power, and the second component of the result is xnx_nxn​.
problems.format: the eigenvalues, larger first; then x₆

problems.html: Let H=(32i−2i3)\mathbf{H}=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 2\mathrm{i}\\ -2\mathrm{i}& 3\end{pmatrix}H=(3−2i​2i3​). (a) Confirm H\mathbf{H}H is Hermitian. (b) Find its eigenvalues (they should be real) and an eigenvector for each. (c) Verify the two eigenvectors are orthogonal under the conjugate inner product u†v=u1‾v1+u2‾v2\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\mathbf{v}=\overline{u_1}v_1+\overline{u_2}v_2u†v=u1​​v1​+u2​​v2​.
hints: Hermitian means the conjugate transpose returns the matrix: transpose it and conjugate every entry, then compare.
For the eigenvalues, note (2i)(−2i)=−4i2=4(2\mathrm{i})(-2\mathrm{i})=-4\mathrm{i}^2=4(2i)(−2i)=−4i2=4, so the characteristic equation is (3−λ)2−4=0(3-\lambda)^2-4=0(3−λ)2−4=0.
For (c), the conjugate inner product conjugates the entries of the first vector before multiplying. The plain dot product would give a different — and misleading — answer.

problems.html: The symmetric matrix A=(31−113−1−1−15)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}3&1&-1\\1&3&-1\\-1&-1&5\end{pmatrix}A=​31−1​13−1​−1−15​​ has eigenvalues λ=2,3,6\lambda=2,3,6λ=2,3,6, with eigenvectors (1,−1,0)T(1,-1,0)^{\mathsf{T}}(1,−1,0)T, (1,1,1)T(1,1,1)^{\mathsf{T}}(1,1,1)T, (1,1,−2)T(1,1,-2)^{\mathsf{T}}(1,1,−2)T respectively. (a) Verify one eigenpair directly, say λ=6\lambda=6λ=6. (b) Confirm the three eigenvectors are mutually orthogonal. (c) Normalise them to build an orthogonal matrix Q\mathbf{Q}Q and write the spectral decomposition A=QDQT\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{Q}^{\mathsf{T}}A=QDQT.
hints: For (a) you need only one matrix–vector multiplication: apply A\mathbf{A}A to the stated eigenvector and check the result is 666 times it.
For (b) take the three pairwise dot products. They must all vanish — guaranteed here, since a symmetric matrix with distinct eigenvalues always has orthogonal eigenvectors.

For (c) divide each eigenvector by its own length to make the columns of Q\mathbf{Q}Q orthonormal; then Q−1=QT\mathbf{Q}^{-1}=\mathbf{Q}^{\mathsf{T}}Q−1=QT, which is what makes the decomposition so convenient.
problems.format: the squared lengths of the three eigenvectors

problems.html: Show that A=(5−113)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}5&-1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}A=(51​−13​) is not diagonalisable.
hints: Start as usual with the characteristic equation and see what is unusual about its roots.
You should find (λ−4)2=0(\lambda-4)^2=0(λ−4)2=0 — a repeated eigenvalue. That alone does not settle it.
Now count independent eigenvectors: work out the rank of A−4I\mathbf{A}-4\mathbf{I}A−4I. One eigenvector for a doubled eigenvalue means defective.

problems.html: A streaming service tracks subscribers. Each month a subscribed user stays subscribed with probability 0.80.80.8 and lapses with 0.20.20.2; a lapsed user resubscribes with 0.40.40.4 and stays lapsed with 0.60.60.6. Let xn=(subscribed, lapsed)\mathbf{x}_n=(\text{subscribed},\,\text{lapsed})xn​=(subscribed,lapsed) fractions. (a) Write the transition matrix P\mathbf{P}P and find its eigenvalues; (b) find the steady-state distribution; (c) starting from everyone subscribed, x0=(1,0)\mathbf{x}_0=(1,0)x0​=(1,0), find a closed form for xn\mathbf{x}_nxn​ and state the long-run subscribed fraction.
hints: Build P\mathbf{P}P so that each column describes where one state goes next — the columns, not the rows, must sum to 111.
Every transition matrix has λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 as an eigenvalue; find the other from the trace, since the two eigenvalues sum to it.

The steady state is the λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 eigenvector scaled so its entries sum to 111. For (c), decompose x0\mathbf{x}_0x0​ in the eigenbasis: the second eigenvalue's contribution decays like 0.4n0.4^n0.4n, which is exactly why the chain settles.
problems.format: the two eigenvalues; then the steady state

problems.html: Find the eigenvalues and an eigenvector of A=(1−221)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}A=(12​−21​). What does the modulus of the eigenvalues say about the orbit of xn+1=Axn\mathbf{x}_{n+1}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_nxn+1​=Axn​?
hints: The characteristic equation is (1−λ)2+4=0(1-\lambda)^2+4=0(1−λ)2+4=0, which has no real solution — expect a complex conjugate pair.
Solve to get λ=1±2i\lambda=1\pm2\mathrm{i}λ=1±2i, then compute ∣λ∣=a2+b2|\lambda|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}∣λ∣=a2+b2​.
Compare ∣λ∣|\lambda|∣λ∣ with 111: bigger means each step scales the vector outwards, so the orbit spirals away from the origin.
problems.format: the modulus of the eigenvalues, to 3 d.p.

problems.html: A data set has (scaled) covariance matrix A=(4221)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}A=(42​21​). (a) Find its eigenvalues and eigenvectors. (b) Confirm the eigenvectors are orthogonal. (c) In PCA terms, along which direction does the data vary, and how much variance lies in the perpendicular direction?
hints: Set up det⁡(A−λI)=0\det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=0det(A−λI)=0 and expand carefully — the constant term is what matters here.
You should get λ2−5λ=0\lambda^2-5\lambda=0λ2−5λ=0, which factorises as λ(λ−5)=0\lambda(\lambda-5)=0λ(λ−5)=0.
A zero eigenvalue means the matrix is singular — check that det⁡A=0\det\mathbf{A}=0detA=0, and think about what that says about the data lying on a line.

problems.html:
State whether each is true or false, with a one-line justification.

  1. Every real 2×22\times22×2 matrix has at least one real eigenvalue.

  2. If A\mathbf{A}A is invertible, 000 is not an eigenvalue of A\mathbf{A}A.

  3. A 3×33\times33×3 matrix with eigenvalues 2,2,52,2,52,2,5 can never be diagonalised.

  4. Eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent.

  5. A real symmetric matrix can have a non-real eigenvalue.

  6. If λ\lambdaλ is an eigenvalue of A\mathbf{A}A, then λ2\lambda^2λ2 is an eigenvalue of A2\mathbf{A}^2A2.
hints: Most of these are settled by an example you have already met in this sheet — the rotation matrix disposes of two of them.
For (b), a zero eigenvalue means some non-zero vector is sent to 0\mathbf{0}0, which is precisely what singular means.

For (c), a repeated eigenvalue only blocks diagonalisation when its eigenspace is too small; diag⁡(2,2,5)\operatorname{diag}(2,2,5)diag(2,2,5) settles it. For (e), remember what the spectral theorem guarantees about symmetric matrices.

problems.html: Suppose Av=λv\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}Av=λv with v≠0\mathbf{v}\neq\mathbf{0}v=0. Show that (a) A2v=λ2v\mathbf{A}^2\mathbf{v}=\lambda^2\mathbf{v}A2v=λ2v; (b) (A+cI)v=(λ+c)v(\mathbf{A}+c\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}=(\lambda+c)\mathbf{v}(A+cI)v=(λ+c)v for any scalar ccc; (c) if A\mathbf{A}A is invertible then λ≠0\lambda\neq0λ=0 and A−1v=1λv\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{v}=\tfrac1\lambda\mathbf{v}A−1v=λ1​v.
hints: For (a), apply A\mathbf{A}A to both sides of Av=λv\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}Av=λv and remember λ\lambdaλ is a scalar, so it slides past A\mathbf{A}A.
For (b), just expand (A+cI)v(\mathbf{A}+c\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}(A+cI)v and collect the v\mathbf{v}v terms.
For the inverse case, start from Av=λv\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}Av=λv and apply A−1\mathbf{A}^{-1}A−1 to both sides. Why must λ≠0\lambda\neq0λ=0 for this to make sense?
problems.format: part (c)'s eigenvalue of A⁻¹ when λ = 4

problems.html: A student finds the eigenvalues of A=(2112)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}A=(21​12​) like this: “(2−λ)2−1=0(2-\lambda)^2-1=0(2−λ)2−1=0, so (2−λ)2=1(2-\lambda)^2=1(2−λ)2=1, hence 2−λ=12-\lambda=12−λ=1, giving λ=1\lambda=1λ=1.” Identify the mistake and give the correct eigenvalues.
hints: Work through the student's algebra yourself and see whether each step follows.
(2−λ)2=1(2-\lambda)^2=1(2−λ)2=1 gives 2−λ=±12-\lambda=\pm12−λ=±1, not just 2−λ=12-\lambda=12−λ=1. What did the student drop?
Taking a square root of both sides of an equation always produces two cases — losing one loses an eigenvalue.

problems.html: Show that a real symmetric matrix A=(abbd)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&d\end{pmatrix}A=(ab​bd​) always has real eigenvalues. (This is the 2×22\times22×2 case of the spectral theorem that underpins the orthogonal diagonalisation in Exercise 2.5.)
hints: Write the characteristic equation for the general symmetric (abbd)\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&d\end{pmatrix}(ab​bd​) and get it into the form λ2−(a+d)λ+(ad−b2)=0\lambda^2-(a+d)\lambda+(ad-b^2)=0λ2−(a+d)λ+(ad−b2)=0.
Real roots are exactly the condition that the discriminant is ≥0\geq 0≥0. Compute it.
The discriminant simplifies to (a−d)2+4b2(a-d)^2+4b^2(a−d)2+4b2 — now say why that can never be negative.
problems.format: the discriminant when a = 1, b = 2, d = 3

problems.html: For each matrix find the eigenvalues and an eigenvector for each (allow complex values, and note any defective case): (a) (6−123),(b) (2−112),(c) (1−113),(d) (0220).\text{(a)}\ \begin{pmatrix}6&-1\\2&3\end{pmatrix},\quad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ \begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},\quad\allowbreak \text{(c)}\ \begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&3\end{pmatrix},\quad\allowbreak \text{(d)}\ \begin{pmatrix}0&2\\2&0\end{pmatrix}.(a) (62​−13​),(b) (21​−12​),(c) (11​−13​),(d) (02​20​).
hints: Form det⁡(A−λI)=0\det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=0det(A−λI)=0 in each case; the trace and determinant give a quick check on the roots.
In (b) the discriminant is negative, so expect a complex conjugate pair — carry on regardless, the method is unchanged.

In (c) the characteristic polynomial is a perfect square. A repeated root is not the end of the story: compute the rank of A−2I\mathbf{A}-2\mathbf{I}A−2I to see how many independent eigenvectors it really has.

problems.html: Find all eigenvalues and an eigenvector for each of A=(120210004)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\2&1&0\\0&0&4\end{pmatrix}A=​120​210​004​​.
hints: Notice the block structure: the third row and column are isolated, so 444 is an eigenvalue immediately.
That leaves the 2×22\times22×2 block (1221)\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}(12​21​) to handle on its own.
Its characteristic equation is (1−λ)2−4=0(1-\lambda)^2-4=0(1−λ)2−4=0.

problems.html: Let A=(0121)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\2&1\end{pmatrix}A=(02​11​). Diagonalise it and find a closed form for An\mathbf{A}^{n}An.
hints: Characteristic equation: λ2−λ−2=0\lambda^2-\lambda-2=0λ2−λ−2=0.
Factorise it, then find an eigenvector for each root to build P\mathbf{P}P.
Finish with An=PDnP−1\mathbf{A}^n=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}^n\mathbf{P}^{-1}An=PDnP−1.

problems.html: Let H=(1i−i1)\mathbf{H}=\begin{pmatrix}1&\mathrm{i}\\-\mathrm{i}&1\end{pmatrix}H=(1−i​i1​). Check it is Hermitian, find its eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and verify the eigenvectors are orthogonal under the conjugate inner product.
hints: Check the Hermitian property first: conjugate every entry, transpose, and compare with the original.
For the eigenvalues use (i)(−i)=1(\mathrm{i})(-\mathrm{i})=1(i)(−i)=1, so the characteristic equation is (1−λ)2−1=0(1-\lambda)^2-1=0(1−λ)2−1=0.
One eigenvalue comes out zero, which tells you the matrix is singular. For the orthogonality check, conjugate the first vector's entries before multiplying.

problems.html: Continuing Exercise 2.4, a student checks whether the eigenvectors v5=(i,1)T\mathbf{v}_5=(\mathrm{i},1)^{\mathsf{T}}v5​=(i,1)T and v1=(−i,1)T\mathbf{v}_1=(-\mathrm{i},1)^{\mathsf{T}}v1​=(−i,1)T of the Hermitian matrix are orthogonal: “v5Tv1=(i)(−i)+(1)(1)=1+1=2≠0\mathbf{v}_5^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{v}_1=(\mathrm{i})(-\mathrm{i})+(1)(1)=1+1=2\neq0v5T​v1​=(i)(−i)+(1)(1)=1+1=2=0, so they are not orthogonal.” Identify the mistake and give the correct verdict.
hints: The arithmetic in the student's line is correct; what is wrong is the inner product being used.
For complex vectors, orthogonality is measured by the conjugate inner product, which conjugates the entries of the first vector before multiplying.

Redo it that way: (i)‾=−i\overline{(\mathrm{i})}=-\mathrm{i}(i)​=−i, so the first term becomes (−i)(−i)=i2=−1(-\mathrm{i})(-\mathrm{i})=\mathrm{i}^2=-1(−i)(−i)=i2=−1. The verdict reverses — as the spectral theorem for Hermitian matrices says it must.
problems.format: the correct value of the conjugate inner product

problems.html: Write down the matrix of the rotation through θ=120∘\theta=120^\circθ=120∘ and state its eigenvalues in the form e±iθ\mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\theta}e±iθ (and as a±bia\pm b\mathrm{i}a±bi).
hints: Substitute θ=120∘\theta=120^\circθ=120∘ into the general rotation matrix, using cos⁡120∘=−12\cos120^\circ=-\tfrac12cos120∘=−21​ and sin⁡120∘=32\sin120^\circ=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}sin120∘=23​​.
You need not compute a characteristic polynomial: a rotation through θ\thetaθ always has eigenvalues e±iθ\mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\theta}e±iθ.

Convert with Euler's formula, e±iθ=cos⁡θ±isin⁡θ\mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\theta}=\cos\theta\pm\mathrm{i}\sin\thetae±iθ=cosθ±isinθ. Both have modulus 111, which records that a rotation changes no lengths.
problems.format: the real part of each eigenvalue, then |λ|

problems.html: For each matrix, give the algebraic and geometric multiplicity of every eigenvalue, and say whether it is diagonalisable: (a) (210020003),(b) (200020003),(c) (4201).\text{(a)}\ \begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\0&2&0\\0&0&3\end{pmatrix},\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ \begin{pmatrix}2&0&0\\0&2&0\\0&0&3\end{pmatrix},\qquad\allowbreak \text{(c)}\ \begin{pmatrix}4&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.(a) ​200​120​003​​,(b) ​200​020​003​​,(c) (40​21​).
hints: Algebraic multiplicity counts how often an eigenvalue repeats as a root; geometric multiplicity counts its independent eigenvectors.
The geometric multiplicity is the nullity of A−λI\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I}A−λI, so compute that matrix's rank and subtract from the size.
A matrix is diagonalisable exactly when the two multiplicities agree for every eigenvalue. Compare (a) and (b): the same eigenvalues, but a different verdict.

problems.html: The symmetric matrix A=(210131012)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\1&3&1\\0&1&2\end{pmatrix}A=​210​131​012​​ (think of it as a covariance matrix) has eigenvalues λ=1,2,4\lambda=1,2,4λ=1,2,4, with eigenvectors (1,−1,1)T(1,-1,1)^{\mathsf{T}}(1,−1,1)T, (1,0,−1)T(1,0,-1)^{\mathsf{T}}(1,0,−1)T, (1,2,1)T(1,2,1)^{\mathsf{T}}(1,2,1)T respectively. (Mirroring Exercise 2.5, the eigenvectors are supplied so the work stays clean.) (a) Verify one eigenpair directly, say λ=4\lambda=4λ=4. (b) Confirm the three eigenvectors are mutually orthogonal. (c) Normalise them to build an orthogonal matrix Q\mathbf{Q}Q and write the spectral decomposition A=QDQT\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{Q}^{\mathsf{T}}A=QDQT. (d) In PCA language, which direction is the first principal axis and what fraction of the total variance does it carry?
hints: For (a) apply A\mathbf{A}A to the stated eigenvector and check you get 444 times it back — one multiplication settles it.
For (c) normalise each eigenvector by dividing by its own length, so that Q\mathbf{Q}Q has orthonormal columns and Q−1=QT\mathbf{Q}^{-1}=\mathbf{Q}^{\mathsf{T}}Q−1=QT.

For (d) the first principal axis is the eigenvector of the largest eigenvalue, and the variance it carries is that eigenvalue as a fraction of the total — which is the sum of all three, that is, the trace.
problems.format: the fraction of the variance on the first axis

problems.html: A two-feature data set has covariance matrix C=(3223)\mathbf{C}=\begin{pmatrix}3&2\\2&3\end{pmatrix}C=(32​23​) (each feature has variance 333; their covariance is 222). (a) Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of C\mathbf{C}C. (b) Which eigenvector is the first principal component? (c) What percentage of the total variance does it capture?
hints: The matrix is symmetric, so expect real eigenvalues and perpendicular eigenvectors.
(3−λ)2−4=0(3-\lambda)^2-4=0(3−λ)2−4=0, so 3−λ=±23-\lambda=\pm23−λ=±2.
The larger eigenvalue's eigenvector is the direction of greatest variance — the first principal component.

problems.html: Revisit the complex-eigenvalue system of Exercise 2.8, xn+1=Axn\mathbf{x}_{n+1}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_nxn+1​=Axn​ with A=(1−221)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}A=(12​−21​) and x0=(1,0)T\mathbf{x}_0=(1,0)^{\mathsf{T}}x0​=(1,0)T. Compute x1,x2,x3\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2,\mathbf{x}_3x1​,x2​,x3​, plot the four points, and sketch the orbit through them. Relate what you draw to the eigenvalues λ=1±2i\lambda=1\pm2\mathrm{i}λ=1±2i.
hints: Just multiply: apply A\mathbf{A}A to x0\mathbf{x}_0x0​, then to the result, and again.
Before plotting, compute the modulus of each point. They should grow by a constant factor at every step.
That factor is ∣λ∣=5|\lambda|=\sqrt5∣λ∣=5​, and the argument of λ\lambdaλ is the angle turned through each step. A modulus greater than 111 means the spiral opens outwards.

problems.html: The Lucas numbers obey Ln+1=Ln+Ln−1L_{n+1}=L_n+L_{n-1}Ln+1​=Ln​+Ln−1​ with L0=2, L1=1L_0=2,\ L_1=1L0​=2, L1​=1 (2,1,3,4,7,11,…2,1,3,4,7,11,\dots2,1,3,4,7,11,…). Using the matrix A=(1110)\mathbf{A}=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)A=(11​10​) with eigenvalues the golden ratio φ=1+52\varphi=\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}φ=21+5​​ and ψ=1−52\psi=\tfrac{1-\sqrt5}{2}ψ=21−5​​ (eigenvectors (φ,1)T,(ψ,1)T(\varphi,1)^{\mathsf{T}},(\psi,1)^{\mathsf{T}}(φ,1)T,(ψ,1)T), show that Ln=φ n+ψ nL_n=\varphi^{\,n}+\psi^{\,n}Ln​=φn+ψn.
hints: Package the recurrence as (Ln+1Ln)=An(L1L0)\begin{pmatrix}L_{n+1}\\L_n\end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{A}^n\begin{pmatrix}L_1\\L_0\end{pmatrix}(Ln+1​Ln​​)=An(L1​L0​​), with the start vector (1,2)T(1,2)^{\mathsf{T}}(1,2)T.
Write that start vector as a(φ,1)T+b(ψ,1)Ta(\varphi,1)^{\mathsf{T}}+b(\psi,1)^{\mathsf{T}}a(φ,1)T+b(ψ,1)T and solve the two equations for aaa and bbb.
Use φ+ψ=1\varphi+\psi=1φ+ψ=1 to simplify: both coefficients come out as 111. Each eigenvector is then scaled by its eigenvalue to the nnn, and the second component gives LnL_nLn​.

problems.html: A two-stage population (juveniles jjj, adults aaa) updates by (ja)n+1=A(ja)n\left(\begin{smallmatrix}j\\a\end{smallmatrix}\right)_{n+1}=\mathbf{A}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}j\\a\end{smallmatrix}\right)_n(ja​)n+1​=A(ja​)n​ with A=(040.50)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}0&4\\0.5&0\end{pmatrix}A=(00.5​40​) (each adult yields 444 juveniles; half the juveniles survive to adulthood). Find the eigenvalues and hence the long-run growth factor per step and the juvenile-to-adult ratio that the model preserves.
hints: The characteristic equation is unusually simple here, because the matrix has zeros on its diagonal.
You should reach λ2−2=0\lambda^2-2=0λ2−2=0, so the eigenvalues are ±2\pm\sqrt2±2​; the growth per step is set by their common modulus.
The ratio the model preserves is the eigenvector of +2+\sqrt2+2​: solve (A−2 I)v=0(\mathbf{A}-\sqrt2\,\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}(A−2​I)v=0 and read it off as juveniles to adults.
problems.format: growth factor, then the j : a ratio, to 3 d.p.

problems.html: A regular Markov chain settles to a unique steady state when λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 occurs just once and every other eigenvalue has modulus less than 111. For each transition matrix, find the eigenvalues and say whether the chain converges or oscillates: (a) P=(0.70.20.30.8),(b) P=(0110).\text{(a)}\ \mathbf{P}=\begin{pmatrix}0.7&0.2\\0.3&0.8\end{pmatrix},\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ \mathbf{P}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.(a) P=(0.70.3​0.20.8​),(b) P=(01​10​).
hints: Find both eigenvalues in each case; every transition matrix has λ=1\lambda=1λ=1, so the trace hands you the other one.
The question is entirely about the second eigenvalue: compare its modulus with 111.

A modulus strictly below 111 makes that mode decay and the chain settle; a modulus equal to 111 means it never dies away. Look at what the second matrix does to a state to see the oscillation directly.

problems.html: Show that a square matrix A\mathbf{A}A and its transpose AT\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{T}}AT have the same eigenvalues.
hints: Compare the two characteristic polynomials det⁡(A−λI)\det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})det(A−λI) and det⁡(AT−λI)\det(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{T}}-\lambda\mathbf{I})det(AT−λI).
Note that (A−λI)T=AT−λI(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})^{\mathsf{T}}=\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{T}}-\lambda\mathbf{I}(A−λI)T=AT−λI, since I\mathbf{I}I is its own transpose.
Now use the fact that transposing does not change a determinant. Note this says nothing about the eigenvectors themselves — those generally differ.
problems.format: do A and Aᵀ have the same eigenvalues?

questions.stem: A 2×22\times22×2 matrix has the repeated eigenvalue λ=4\lambda=4λ=4. Is it diagonalisable?
options: Yes — every square matrix with a real eigenvalue is diagonalisable.
Yes, provided the matrix is invertible.
No — a repeated eigenvalue always blocks diagonalisation.
Not enough information: it depends on how many independent eigenvectors λ=4\lambda=4λ=4 has.
questions.hint: The repeated eigenvalue is only half the story. Compare 4I4\mathbf{I}4I with (4104)\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\0&4\end{pmatrix}(40​14​) — both have λ=4\lambda=4λ=4 twice.
questions.why: A repeated eigenvalue is a warning, not a verdict. What matters is the geometric multiplicity — the number of independent eigenvectors, which is the nullity of A−4I\mathbf{A}-4\mathbf{I}A−4I. If that is 222 the matrix is diagonalisable (indeed A=4I\mathbf{A}=4\mathbf{I}A=4I); if it is 111 the matrix is defective. Invertibility is irrelevant: (4104)\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\0&4\end{pmatrix}(40​14​) is invertible and not diagonalisable.

questions.stem: The rotation R=(0−110)\mathbf{R}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}R=(01​−10​) has eigenvalues ±i\pm\mathrm{i}±i. What does having no real eigenvalue mean geometrically?
options: The rotation must be by more than 180∘180^\circ180∘.
The matrix is singular, so it collapses the plane to a line.
No real direction is preserved — every vector is genuinely turned.
The matrix has no eigenvectors of any kind.
questions.hint: A real eigenvector would be a direction the map merely stretches. Picture a quarter-turn of the plane and try to find one.
questions.why: A real eigenvector would be a direction the map merely stretches. A quarter-turn moves every direction, so no such real direction exists — which is exactly what a complex-conjugate pair of eigenvalues records. The matrix is not singular (det⁡R=1\det\mathbf{R}=1detR=1), and it does have eigenvectors: they simply live in C2\mathbb{C}^2C2 rather than R2\mathbb{R}^2R2.

questions.stem: Why is v=0\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}v=0 excluded from the definition of an eigenvector?
options: Because eigenvalues must be non-zero.
Because A0=λ0\mathbf{A}\mathbf{0}=\lambda\mathbf{0}A0=λ0 holds for every λ\lambdaλ, so it would tell us nothing.
Because the zero vector has no length.
Because A0\mathbf{A}\mathbf{0}A0 is undefined.
questions.hint: Put v=0\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}v=0 into Av=λv\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}Av=λv and ask which values of λ\lambdaλ satisfy it.
questions.why: A0=0=λ0\mathbf{A}\mathbf{0}=\mathbf{0}=\lambda\mathbf{0}A0=0=λ0 is true for every scalar λ\lambdaλ whatsoever. Admitting 0\mathbf{0}0 would make every number an eigenvalue of every matrix, and the definition would carry no information. Note that eigenvalues themselves may perfectly well be zero — that happens exactly when A\mathbf{A}A is singular.

questions.stem: You compute eigenvalues λ1=3, λ2=5\lambda_1=3,\ \lambda_2=5λ1​=3, λ2​=5 for a matrix with trace 999. What should you conclude?
options: Nothing is wrong; the trace is unrelated to the eigenvalues.
There is an arithmetic error: the eigenvalues must sum to the trace.
The matrix is not diagonalisable.
The remaining eigenvalue must be 111.
questions.hint: There is a one-line check relating the eigenvalues to the trace. Add the two you have.
questions.why: For an n×nn\times nn×n matrix the eigenvalues sum to the trace and multiply to the determinant. Here 3+5=8≠93+5=8\neq93+5=8=9, so something has gone wrong — most often a sign slip in expanding det⁡(A−λI)\det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})det(A−λI). This is the cheapest check available and is worth doing every single time.

questions.stem: In a diagonalisation A=PDP−1\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{P}^{-1}A=PDP−1, what must be true of the order of the columns of P\mathbf{P}P?
options: They must be in increasing order of eigenvalue.
They must be normalised to unit length.
The order does not matter at all.
The order is free, but must match the order of the eigenvalues down D\mathbf{D}D.
questions.hint: Multiply out AP=PD\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}AP=PD and read what it says one column at a time.
questions.why: Any ordering of the eigenvectors gives a valid diagonalisation, but the kkk-th column of P\mathbf{P}P must be an eigenvector for the kkk-th diagonal entry of D\mathbf{D}D. Swapping one without the other breaks the identity. Normalising is optional for diagonalisation in general — it matters for the orthogonal diagonalisation of a symmetric matrix, where P−1=PT\mathbf{P}^{-1}=\mathbf{P}^{\mathsf{T}}P−1=PT requires orthonormal columns.

questions.stem: A Markov chain's transition matrix always has λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 as an eigenvalue. What does the corresponding eigenvector represent?
options: A distribution left unchanged by one step — the steady state.
The starting distribution of the chain.
The fastest-decaying mode of the chain.
The direction in which the chain grows without bound.
questions.hint: Write out what Pv=1⋅v\mathbf{P}\mathbf{v}=1\cdot\mathbf{v}Pv=1⋅v says about applying one step of the chain to v\mathbf{v}v.
questions.why: Pv=1⋅v\mathbf{P}\mathbf{v}=1\cdot\mathbf{v}Pv=1⋅v says precisely that applying one step leaves v\mathbf{v}v unchanged, which is what a steady state is. Scaled so its entries sum to 111, it is the long-run distribution. Nothing grows without bound: the other eigenvalues have modulus below 111 for a regular chain, so their contributions die away and the λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 direction is what survives.

questions.stem: S\mathbf{S}S is a real symmetric matrix. What does that guarantee about its eigenvalues?
options: They are all real.
They are all real, and always distinct.
They may be complex, as for a rotation.
They are all real and positive.
questions.hint: Three different claims are being run together here: real, positive, and distinct. Symmetry buys exactly one of them — try to break the other two with a small example.
questions.why: A real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues, and eigenvectors belonging to different eigenvalues are orthogonal. That is all symmetry gives, and the two overreaches are easy to break. Positivity fails for (0110)\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}(01​10​), which is symmetric with eigenvalues ±1\pm1±1; positivity is a further condition, called positive definiteness. Distinctness fails for the identity, symmetric with the eigenvalue 111 twice. Complex eigenvalues genuinely do occur — the rotation of this unit has ±i\pm\mathrm{i}±i — but a rotation is not symmetric, which is exactly why it is allowed them.

questions.stem: For complex vectors, orthogonality is tested with u†v=u1‾v1+u2‾v2\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\mathbf{v}=\overline{u_{1}}v_{1}+\overline{u_{2}}v_{2}u†v=u1​​v1​+u2​​v2​ rather than u1v1+u2v2u_{1}v_{1}+u_{2}v_{2}u1​v1​+u2​v2​. Why the conjugate?
options: Because the conjugate makes every inner product real.
Without it, u†u\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\mathbf{u}u†u need not be a positive real number, so it could not measure a length.
It is only a convention; the two tests agree in every case.
Because a complex matrix is never symmetric.
questions.hint: Try both versions on the single vector u=(1,i)\mathbf{u}=(1,\mathrm{i})u=(1,i), and ask which one returns a sensible squared length.
questions.why: Take u=(1,i)\mathbf{u}=(1,\mathrm{i})u=(1,i). Without the conjugate, 1⋅1+i⋅i=1−1=01\cdot1+\mathrm{i}\cdot\mathrm{i}=1-1=01⋅1+i⋅i=1−1=0, so a perfectly good non-zero vector would come out with zero length and be orthogonal to itself. With the conjugate, ∣1∣2+∣i∣2=2\left|1\right|^{2}+\left|\mathrm{i}\right|^{2}=2∣1∣2+∣i∣2=2, which is what a squared length should look like — and the pattern echoes ∣z∣2=z‾z\left|z\right|^{2}=\overline{z}z∣z∣2=zz from Unit 3. So the two tests certainly do not agree. Complex symmetric matrices exist; the useful class here is the Hermitian one, A†=A\mathbf{A}^{\dagger}=\mathbf{A}A†=A. And u†v\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\mathbf{v}u†v is not real in general — it satisfies u†v=v†u‾\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\mathbf{v}=\overline{\mathbf{v}^{\dagger}\mathbf{u}}u†v=v†u, which forces only u†u\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\mathbf{u}u†u to be real.

questions.stem: Av=3v\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}=3\mathbf{v}Av=3v for some non-zero v\mathbf{v}v. What is A2v\mathbf{A}^{2}\mathbf{v}A2v?
options: 9v9\mathbf{v}9v
3v3\mathbf{v}3v
6v6\mathbf{v}6v
It cannot be determined without knowing A\mathbf{A}A itself.
questions.hint: Apply A\mathbf{A}A twice, one step at a time, using what you are told at each step.
questions.why: Apply A\mathbf{A}A twice: A2v=A(Av)=A(3v)=3(Av)=3⋅3v=9v\mathbf{A}^{2}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{A}(3\mathbf{v})=3(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v})=3\cdot3\mathbf{v}=9\mathbf{v}A2v=A(Av)=A(3v)=3(Av)=3⋅3v=9v. The eigenvector goes through untouched and only the eigenvalue is transformed — squaring the matrix squares the eigenvalue. The same one-eigenvector-at-a-time reading gives A−1v=13v\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{v}=\tfrac13\mathbf{v}A−1v=31​v and (A+kI)v=(3+k)v(\mathbf{A}+k\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}=(3+k)\mathbf{v}(A+kI)v=(3+k)v: powers, shifts and inverses all keep the eigenvectors, which is what makes diagonalisation worth the trouble. Doubling would be the answer to 2Av2\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}2Av, a different question, and no further knowledge of A\mathbf{A}A is needed.
